name: Colin Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on site by seven, usually a commercial fit-out in the city centre, offices or shops, with Brennan Electrical, about forty sparks on the books. Today it was second fix on a dental clinic: hanging lights, terminating sockets, labelling the board. I like the bit where you switch on and the whole floor comes alive. What wears me out is the waiting, standing around because the plasterers are behind and the foreman wants us to look busy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Jo, she's a nurse on nights half the time, in a flat we bought two years ago. We put down a big deposit because I saved hard through my apprenticeship, and there's still about eight months of money in the bank. I'm a union member, I go to the branch meetings, and I still write my jobs in a paper diary because I don't trust the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year there's some new gadget that's going to change the trade, and every year I'm still pulling cable through ceilings by hand. At the branch meeting I'd say the real fight is still pay rates and agency labour, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I don't like change much, I'll admit that, and I like knowing what my week looks like. If the only thing AI does is write the foreman's emails, that's no skin off my nose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep working at Brennan, keep putting a few hundred a month into savings, and keep paying extra off the mortgage when there's overtime. Maybe I'd finally do the inspection and testing course that the union keeps pushing, because that's proper paper that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world I already know, which suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the paper diary. If the firm pushed an app on you anyway, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if they made me, but I'd moan about it. Last year they brought in a timesheet app and I still hand my paper sheet to Gary in the office every Friday. He types it in for me and calls me a dinosaur, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you about the next few years, even with AI out of the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual stuff. Commercial work goes in waves, and when offices stop being built, the agency lads get let go first and then it's us. But I've got my savings and Jo's wage, so even a slow year wouldn't sink us.

say: I'd tell the branch that the **real fight** is still pay rates and agency labour.
I'd say every new gadget was meant to change the trade, and I'm **still pulling cable** by hand.
think: I'd honestly be **relieved**, because I like knowing what my week looks like.
If AI only writes the foreman's emails, it doesn't touch **my work** at all.
do: Keep working at **Brennan Electrical** and paying extra off the mortgage from overtime.
Put a few hundred a month into **savings** as I do now.
Think about the union's **inspection and testing** course because the qualification lasts.
feel: **Calm**, because it looks like the world I already know.
S0.quote: Every year there's some new gadget that's going to change the trade, and every year I'm still pulling cable through ceilings by hand.
fieldNote: Colin's **distrust of apps** is practical, not political: he still hands in a paper timesheet.
His only live worry is the **commercial build cycle**, which he feels covered against by savings and his partner's wage.
Union life frames his public talk; **pay and agency labour** come before technology.

steps.text: Keep working second fix on city fit-outs at Brennan Electrical
Pay overtime money off the flat's mortgage every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should be worried, not us. Nobody's writing an email that can terminate a three-phase board. But I'd also say at the branch that if robots are coming later, we need rules about it written now, while we still have some say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it'd bother me more than I'd let on. If the offices we fit out need fewer staff, there's fewer fit-outs, and that's my bread and butter. I'm not the best spark at Brennan, I'm middle of the pack, so when work dries up I'm not first to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally do that testing and inspection course, because testing is something you need a licensed person for. I'd put the overtime money into savings rather than the holiday Jo wants. And I'd get on the union's working group about technology, even though I'm no expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own hands are fine, but the jobs those hands go to might thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you think would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimators and the office lot, first. Gary does our timesheets and orders, and if software does that, Gary's gone, and he's got two kids. Then the agency lads on site, because they're the first to be cut whenever there's less work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push the union to do anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want a deal saying any robot on site works under a licensed electrician, and that firms tell us a year ahead before they cut. I don't trust bosses to share the savings unless someone makes them.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** should worry before ours, because software can't terminate a board.
I'd tell the branch we need **rules about robots** written now, while we still have a say.
think: Fewer office staff means **fewer fit-outs**, and fit-outs are my bread and butter.
I'm **middle of the pack** at Brennan, so I wouldn't be first to stay in a slow patch.
do: Sign up for the **inspection and testing** course, which needs a licensed person.
Save the **overtime money** instead of spending it on the holiday Jo wants.
Join the union's **technology working group** even without being an expert.
feel: **Uneasy**, because my hands are fine but the work they go to might **thin out**.
S1.quote: Nobody's writing an email that can terminate a three-phase board.
fieldNote: Colin sees the risk as **indirect**: fewer office workers means fewer office fit-outs for his firm.
His instinct is to **organise**, asking for licensed supervision of robots and a year's warning of cuts.
He worries first about **Gary in the office**, who has two kids, before himself.

steps.text: Book the union's inspection and testing course before spring
Put overtime pay into savings instead of a summer holiday
Join the union branch working group on site technology

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd be posting that the government needs to have a plan for all the people who lose office jobs, and that firms using AGI should pay into something for the rest of us. At work I'd be saying that the trades have three years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. If every office worker loses their job in 2028, nobody's paying for new offices, kitchens or rewires, so my work drops off before any robot touches a cable. Then in 2031 the robots turn up anyway, and I'm thirty-two with a mortgage and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and build up cash instead, maybe a year's worth. I'd get the testing course and anything else that needs a licence and a signature. And I'd be at every union meeting pushing for a deal on licensed supervision, because that's the one thing that might keep us in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing, and I'm not someone who changes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo the night you realised this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jo that her job's safer than mine for once, because you can't send a robot to calm a scared old man on a ward at three in the morning. Then I'd say we hold off on the second bedroom we wanted to build. We'd sit at the kitchen table and go through the bank app line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid risk. Would you take any big step, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait on the big stuff, I think. I don't want to throw my savings at a new trade that the robots will also do by 2031. So I'd keep my head down, save, and lean on the union, which I know isn't much of a plan.

say: I'd say the government needs a **plan** for people losing office jobs.
I'd say firms using AGI should **pay into** something for everyone else.
I'd tell the lads that the trades have **three years**, not forever.
think: When office workers lose jobs, nobody pays for **fit-outs or rewires**, so my work drops first.
By 2031 the **robots** come anyway, and I'll be thirty-two with a **mortgage**.
do: Stop overpaying the mortgage and build **a year of cash**.
Get every qualification that needs a **licence and signature**, starting with testing.
Push the union for a deal on **licensed supervision** of robots.
feel: **Scared**, because two years is very little for someone who changes slowly.
S2.quote: If every office worker loses their job in 2028, nobody's paying for new offices, kitchens or rewires, so my work drops off before any robot touches a cable.
fieldNote: Colin spots the **demand shock** before the robot one: his clients lose income first.
He admits his plan is mostly **waiting and saving**, which sits uneasily with how loud he'd be in public.
His partner's **nursing job** now looks like the household's anchor, which he finds strange.
Mood is anxious, not alarmed: his **savings** and her wage give the household some control.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the mortgage and build a year of cash
Finish the inspection and testing licence course this year
Push the union branch for licensed supervision of site robots
Put off building the second bedroom until things settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got time to fight for it properly. I'd be campaigning for a law that says electrical work has to be signed off by a licensed person, robot or not. I'd be telling the younger apprentices to join the union now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking AI, eight for the robots, that's 2034, so I'd be thirty-five. That's still young, which is the frightening bit, because there's a whole career after it. But it's enough time to get my testing ticket and maybe my supervisor's ticket too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the testing course straight away and then the supervisor course in year two. I'd keep saving but I'd still build the second bedroom, because the house is worth more with it. And I'd go to the union's lobbying day at parliament, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but less trapped than with two years. Like there's a ladder there, if I climb it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real gap, two years against five. With two years I'd just sit there. The extra time lets a slow person like me catch up, so I'd be doing the courses instead of watching the bank app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever consider leaving the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not want to. My dad was a postman and he got moved around by every new machine, and he hated it. If the trade goes, I'd rather be the one checking the robots' work than learning to code at thirty-five.

say: I'd campaign for a law that electrical work needs a **licensed sign-off**, robot or not.
I'd tell young apprentices to **join the union** now.
think: Robots by **2034** means I'm thirty-five, with a whole career still ahead.
Five years is **enough time** to get my testing and supervisor tickets.
do: Do the **testing course** now and the **supervisor course** in year two.
Keep saving but still build the **second bedroom**, since it adds value.
Go to the union's **lobbying day** for the first time.
feel: **Uneasy**, but less trapped, because there's a ladder to climb.
Some dread at having a **whole career** left after robots arrive.
S3.quote: The extra time lets a slow person like me catch up, so I'd be doing the courses instead of watching the bank app.
fieldNote: Colin calls himself **slow to change**, and the extra years matter most for exactly that reason.
He'd move from **waiting** to **climbing**: testing, then supervisor tickets.
His father's experience as a **postman** shapes his dislike of being moved around by machines.

steps.text: Get the testing ticket now and supervisor ticket in year two
Go to the union's lobbying day on licensed sign-off rules
Keep saving monthly while building the second bedroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for governments to get it right, so no excuses. I'd want the union pushing for retraining money and a shorter week, so the gains get shared. People would probably think I'm being dramatic, but I'd say it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then three more for robots, so 2039. I'd be forty, probably with kids by then. It's far enough off that I'd mostly carry on, but close enough that I'd be thinking about it every time I sign a test certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the testing and supervisor tickets over the next few years, at my own pace. I'd keep building the savings, and Jo and I would probably still go ahead with kids. I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever has a real plan for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back of my mind. It's the kind of worry that sits there while you're up a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you change anything at all right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still use my paper diary, I'd still do my jobs. The only real change is that I'd stop thinking of this trade as safe forever, and I'd plan for the second half of my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully running a small team, checking work and signing it off. Maybe the robots pull the cable and I'm the one who tests the work and puts my name on it. That's the version I could live with.

say: I'd say ten years leaves governments **no excuses** for getting it wrong.
I'd want the union pushing for **retraining money** and a **shorter week**.
think: Robots by **2039** means I'd be forty, probably with kids.
It's far enough off to **carry on**, but I'd think of it at every test certificate.
do: Get the **testing and supervisor** tickets over a few years at my own pace.
Keep building **savings** and go ahead with **children** with Jo.
Vote for whoever has a real **retraining plan**.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, like a worry up a ladder.
S4.quote: Maybe the robots pull the cable and I'm the one who tests the work and puts my name on it. That's the version I could live with.
fieldNote: With ten years, Colin's plan barely changes; he wants **policy**, not personal upheaval.
He imagines his future as the **licensed signature** on robot work.
He would still start a **family**, a sign that the long horizon calms him.

steps.text: Take the testing and supervisor tickets over the next few years
Vote for the party with a real retraining plan
Start trying for children with Jo as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time for a slow learner like me. What would help is a law that says a licensed electrician has to sign off any electrical work, whoever or whatever does it, and real money for retraining that doesn't come out of my own savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If robots do our jobs, someone's saving a fortune, and I'd want to know it isn't all going to the same few people at the top. A trade is something you own in your hands, and I'd hate to see that taken without a fight.

headlineQuote: A trade is something you own in your hands, and I'd hate to see that taken without a fight.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** commercial electrician at Brennan Electrical who lives with Jo, a nurse, in a flat they bought.
He keeps a **paper diary**, avoids apps and calls himself slow to change.
His union membership shapes his answers: he wants **licensed sign-off** rules and shared gains.
He feels safe in AI Plateau but sees office job losses cutting **fit-out work** first under faster AI.
More warning time turns his plan from **saving and waiting** into steady retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time for someone who learns slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **licensed electrician** to sign off all electrical work.
Public **retraining money** that doesn't come out of his own savings.
